preview: Interview experience of Warren Jacinto for an internship at Goldman Sachs, detailing the online assessment, technical and HR rounds, and final selection.
content:
Interview Experience
Warren Jacinto - TY BTech CE, 221070029
Introduction
I am Warren Jacinto, currently in my third year of pursuing a BTech Degree in Computer
Engineering at Veermata Jijabai Technological Institute, Matunga.
This report will serve as a record of my experience interviewing with Goldman Sachs.

Pre-Placement Talk
Somewhere around 12 July 2024, we received an email from TPO informing us that
Goldman Sachs was visiting the campus for intern hiring. In this email, there were links for
applying on the official Goldman Sachs Careers page as well as details for a webinar.
Platform: Zoom Webinar
Time: 23 July 2024, 5pm - 6pm
The Pre-Placement Talk was engaging and to the point. They started off by explaining what
GS does, why GS stands out from the rest and what kind of lifestyle you can expect at GS.
Pay close attention to whatever is discussed in this meeting, as it serves as a good way to
understand the kind of people the firm is looking for. Additionally, during your interviews,
the interviewers may ask you questions about the firm, and paying attention here, will pay
off then.

Online Assessment
Participants: Everyone who had applied
Test Platform: Hackerrank - video, and screen proctored.
It's been too long to remember the exact format of the OA, but there were 2 sections, one
was coding, and the other was MCQs.
The coding questions were easy, even for me who had relatively less experience with DSA
at that point(~200 LC solved). I can't recall the exact questions, but they were array/maths
based.
The MCQs were a little harder, they were based on a wide variety of topics studied in our
syllabus like: DSA, OOPS, Debugging. The questions were very much doable, it was the time
that was an issue. As long as your CS Fundamentals are clear, this won't be hard.
Throughout this period, your camera and microphone must be on and your screen will be
shared. Make sure you do not under any circumstances: switch tabs, have another
person in your webcam, look away from the screen, speak anything. Your face should
be clearly visible and well lit.
Trust me, the OA is not that difficult and doesn’t even warrant any kind of malpractice, it’s
just not worth the risk. Instead, prepare well and you’ll do fine.
Results: 27 people were shortlisted for interviews, and I was one of them. We received the
results on 25 July 2024, in the afternoon, and I wasted no time starting my preparation.

Interview Day
Date: 26 July 2024
Venue: TPO Seminar Hall
We were asked to report at 8.30 am, and the Pre-Interview Talk was scheduled to begin at
9 am. Additionally we were also asked to bring 3 - 4 printouts of our resumes and dress in
formal attire. I wore a dark blue full sleeves shirt, along with black trousers, a belt and black
formal shoes. For financial firms, your attire matters a lot, so dress well.
GS had sent around 6 -7 people to handle the entire process, of which, ~5 were technical
people, engineers at GS, and the remaining were more HR/Manager types.
During the talk, they gave us an overview of the entire process they were conducting and
their roles at GS. They mentioned that there would be technical rounds, followed by HR
rounds. Then, after the talk concluded, without much further delay, the interview process
commenced around 10 am.
Now, a couple of things to note, before I explain the actual interview experience,
1. Address them respectfully. I always defaulted to “Sir”/”Ma’am”, but if they ask you
to use their first names, then do that.
2. Pay attention to the Pre Interview Talk. Their introductions, their roles at GS,
memorise all that you can, you never know which interviewer you may get. Being
able to recollect all of this about your interviewers will come in handy during the
interview.
3. Try to Answer. If they engage in a Q/A, or just ask any questions in general, try to
answer, because mostly none of the other candidates seated beside you will, and
this will let you stand out.

Round 1 [Technical]
Even though interviews commenced at 10 am, I didn’t have my first round until ~3pm!.
This was incredibly nerve-wracking as there were people who had finished 3 rounds, and I still
hadn’t had my first round yet.
Finally however, I was called for my first technical interview. I sat down across from my
interviewer, and he introduced himself and the role he had at GS. Then, he asked for my
introduction. I gave him the introduction I had memorised when Ayaan/Raunak took my
mock interview. You can find it here. Make sure to memorise a good introduction. Keep it
short and to the point, and don’t be too technical, include some hobbies too, or maybe an
interesting fact. Practise good eye contact and body language.
Then after asking me which language I was comfortable with(C++), he gave me the first
question and a piece of pen and paper to solve it on.
Find Length of Maximum Mountain in an array.
Given an array, say, 4,5,7,8,9,3,6,8,3
Find the length of the largest mountain, that is the maximum distance between points
where the array starts increasing and stops decreasing.
Here the largest mountain would be from i = 0 to 5, length = 5
Note i = 5 to 8 is also a mountain, but not as big as the previous mountain.
I don't remember the approach I gave, but it was some kind of two pointer, nothing too
complicated, and after I explained with an example, he was satisfied and asked me to write
code for it.
Find First Duplicate Character in a String.
Given a string, s = “abcdefghijkalmnopqrst”
Find the index of the first repeating character in the string. Here it is i = 11, ‘a’.
This question is pretty straightforward and I explained a HashSet / unordered_set approach
to solving it, and he was satisfied, telling me code was not necessary.
Client Server Architecture
Then the DSA part concluded, and he took a look at my resume. I was ready for some
questions on the Deep Learning projects I had, or maybe even my GSoC ‘24 project. But I
don’t think he had experience with either DL, or was familiar with GSoC. So he chose to ask
me some questions about Client Server Architecture for Web Applications. He asked quite a
few questions, of which I only remember one.
“Given a client - server web app, the client needs to display the progress of a running job on
the server, and the progress must be real time. How would the client fetch the data from
the server for this?”
I proceeded to explain HTTP Requests and why they were a bad fit for this, since you can’t
have a client making 100s of requests a second to get real time data from the server.
Then, I explained what WebSockets were and why WebSockets were a better fit for the
problem. He was pretty happy with my explanation.

Conclusion of Interview 1
I’d argue the conclusion of the interview is the most important part, because it’s your last
chance to improve the interviewer’s opinion of you.
From what I had observed, each interviewer had a copy of our resume that we had
submitted, and were making notes/marking us on the back of our resumes. Then at the
end, they would give it to the HR person coordinating the process to decide whether to
send us for further interviews or to reject us.
What I’m trying to convey is that the interviewers usually don’t have any absolute scale by
which to measure you.
As much as possible, try to connect with the interviewer. Whether you’re from the same
village, same school, or have the same shirt. Try to “vibe” with them.
You get the chance to do this at the end of the interview, when they ask you, “Do you have
any questions for me?”.
Never ask for feedback on your responses. Not only are they not allowed to give that
(most of the time), it reflects badly on their perception of you.
Always ask something though, don’t say “No, I do not” and miss out on this chance. Make
that question a good one, it should be unique, and not something generic everyone else
asks. This is where the attention you paid during the Pre Placement Talk, and the Pre
Interview Talk pays off.
I started off by asking him about what his division(memorised from the Pre Interview Talk)
did at GS. He went on for 5 minutes explaining what he did and how long he had been
doing it. I then followed up with “But, is that the division you always wanted to end up in?
Didn’t you ever want to switch?” and “How good is the internal mobility at GS, when it
comes to switching projects/divisions?”. This conversation continued for like 10 minutes
and I was able to connect with him, to the point where I guess even he had forgotten it was
an interview and I was much more relaxed too.
After ending with a thank you, I left the room, at that moment, uncertain of my
performance. I then went to grab a snack from the canteen as I hadn’t had lunch and met
some friends.

Round 2 [Technical + HR]:
Now, a lot of people had 3 interviews, 2 Technical followed by 1 HR, but I had only 2
interviews, 1 Technical and 1 Technical + HR. I'm not sure how to classify the last round, as I
had all kinds of questions.
But one thing was certain, all of us had our last round with this person who I'll name “Anish”
for anonymity. He seemed to be the person in charge of the entire process and everybody
had their final round with him. He was clearly someone who started off as a technical
person and graduated to a managerial position, based on the questions he asked us.
At ~5pm, I sat down across from Anish and he had a very “chill” vibe to him. We exchanged
introductions. He asked me where my interests were, in Computer Engineering. I
mentioned my love of Operating Systems and Low Level Programming, alongside GPU
Programming, and took this as an opportunity to mention my GSoC ‘24 project too.
After hearing this mixture of topics, he asked me a couple of questions:
I don't remember the exact wording, but he asked me about what the OS does, and more
importantly about the device management part. He asked me how so many different kinds
of devices are able to interface with an OS, what are drivers?, among other questions.
Then, the conversation went on a tangent towards GPUs and I don't remember exactly
what we talked about, but it was something related to how GPUs are used on a large scale.
I do know that I was able to answer everything properly, because all of these are my
favourite parts of Computer Science.
“Imagine you have to design a ticketing app like IRCTC’s UTS app. How do you handle 1000s
of users trying to book the same tickets? Be aware that on UTS, you receive the tickets only
after payment, and if for some reason, the booking fails, you are refunded within 7 days.
Come up with a solution to improve this system.”
First I answered regarding the 1000s of concurrent users on the platform accessing the
same resource. I mentioned a kind of “Lock-Out” mechanism, where anyone booking a
ticket had exclusive access to it for, say, 2 minutes, to confirm and complete payment, and
nobody else could access the same seats in this window. I also came up with some other
solutions which I’m unable to recall at the time of writing. We had a long back and forth on
this topic and possible solutions, with him constantly poking at my ideas, asking me “How
would it work in XYZ situation?”, and “Could it work in ABC case?”.
After this, he seemed pretty happy with my answers, and gave a solution he came up with
on the spot, which was a kind of “Hold Out” mechanism, similar to what Uber/Ola use,
where money is debited from your account and held by the bank, but not credited to IRCTC,
until the booking is confirmed. If for some reason, it is not confirmed, the money goes
straight back to your account, without need for a 7 day wait period for IRCTC to refund you.
It was at this point I realised, this wasn’t a planned question, but rather something he came
up with on the spot, and something he wanted us to solve together.
Finally, he asked me about my background, my family, why I came to VJTI, why I did not try
for any NIT/IIT, to which I replied with the truth.
There’s a lot of gaps in my memory regarding that round, but from what I remember, he
was essentially trying to see how good my communication skills were, alongside my ability
to think on the spot.
It’s one thing to be good at problem solving, but if you can’t explain your ideas to
others who are not as knowledgeable as you, then it's absolutely worthless.
This is where I got tremendously lucky as I had a ton of practice with my communication
skills during the Project X meets.

Results
I went back to the TPO hall, much more relaxed now that the interview was over. I sat and
joked with friends who had also finished their interviews until somewhere around 6pm.
Then, the team from GS came into the hall and announced that they were done with
interviews and because Swapnil Sir requested, they were declaring the results on the spot.
One by one each of the names were called in alphabetical order, and at the very end, my
name was called too.
They selected 6 people:
1. Alinaa Bharde
2. Druhi Phutane
3. Manav Shah
4. Mohammed Bhadsorawala
5. Sneha Menat
6. Warren Jacinto
Initially I was a bit confused as I thought she meant to say “Varun” who was also a
candidate, and not everyone gets my name right on the first try. But nope, she meant me.
We all exchanged congratulations and to say I was overjoyed would be an understatement.
All of us then left the TPO hall, and the first thing I did, while exiting the Mech Gate was call
my Mom and Dad and tell them the news.
I went home extremely relaxed as the biggest challenge of the Third Year of any BTech
degree was over, and I could stop grinding DSA(which I hated doing).

Resources and Tips
There is no one perfect interview preparation guide, but here’s what I did.
Get really really good at atleast one core language
For me, this was C and C++. When I say good, I mean really good, to the point where you
know the ins and outs of the languages. I got good at C thanks to my GSoC project which
was entirely in C and I got good at C++ because it was the first language I learnt.
If you want a reference for what I mean when I say good, I mean templates and
virtual/static methods, C++ StdLib, iterators, lambdas, streams, etc in C++, and, void *
and its appropriate usage, struct alignments, shared libs, static/dynamic linking, system calls,
mmap, etc, in C.
Most of this I learnt online, through cppreference.com and similar sites. But the other more
niche stuff, I learnt through practice.
Java/Python are also good choices, though I’d recommend Java over Python.
Make sure your CS Fundamentals are super strong
This includes OS, OOPS, DBMS, LLD, DSA, etc. I got lucky because my DBMS is atrocious and
I wasn’t asked a single DBMS question, but if you want to be thoroughly prepared, do
everything properly. You’ll find resources in CoC’s guide.
Practise DSA regularly
I started my DSA prep relatively earlier compared to others, and I used Neetcode 150 as my
reference, finishing the entire sheet well before GS came to our college.
Be consistent in your DSA prep, don’t give up quickly and look at the solution, struggle a
little bit, it’s natural and I did it too. Make sure you look at the most optimised solutions
after you solve them.
Improve your English Speaking and Communication skills
I lucked out in this aspect, because I speak English with my family at home and have done
so since I was born. I also read quite a lot of crime fiction novels when I was younger. Your
accent, the way you pronounce words, the intonation you use, the pauses, the uhm’s the
ahh’s, all of it is the first thing the interviewer looks at. Make sure it's proper. The best way
to improve is by doing, so practise with your friends.
When it comes to communication skills, it helps a lot if you're a part of any club or
community and have had to organise events in a team with others. Otherwise you can look
online on youtube for ways to improve. You should be able to explain an idea you have to
someone with no knowledge of it and have them understand it to the same degree you do.
Build a good resume
My resume at the time of Goldman Sachs is here. This is hands down the best template for
a LaTeX resume. CoC’s guide for making a good resume should be more than enough. Get
your resume reviewed by senior’s as soon as you can and incorporate their feedback. I was
fortunate enough to get this feedback from Project X seniors pretty early, way before the
internship season started.
Be calm
I understand how incredibly scary it is when you give your first interview. I was surrounded
by all these people who were arguably so much better qualified than I was. But it’s
extremely important you never show this nervousness to anyone. On the outside, you need
to be cool, calm and collected. Respond with confidence when asked a question. Don't
break under the pressure. Remember, no matter what it may look like, the other
candidates are just as terrified, if not more, than you and the interviewers are rooting for
you, they want you to succeed, and will never intentionally try to fail you.
Prepare Well
Most of the time, TPO receives the interview shortlist by afternoon/evening on the day
before the interviews. So if you proceed with the mentality that “I’ll study OOPS, OS when i
actually get shortlisted and will do DSA for now, so I can focus on getting shortlisted” Then
you’ll be sorely underprepared for the interviews, as one day is not nearly enough to do
everything well. So alongside DSA, keep doing CS fundamentals as well. Research about the
company visiting, what they do, their rank among similar companies, the role you are
applying for, the JD associated with it and everything else as soon as you can before going
for interviews. Go through CoC’s archive of past interview experiences, for at least the
previous 2-3 years to get a good idea about what the company asks in terms of coding and
puzzles
Give Mocks
CoC usually organises mock interviews for those who take an active part in CoC activities
where seniors guide you about how to give interviews. These are extremely important and
should be taken seriously, as the feedback you get from your mock interviews will matter a
lot. If you don’t get seniors to take your mocks, ask your friends to help you out.
Conclusion
In conclusion, if there's anything you should take away from this, it is the points in the
previous section.
If you are not selected, don’t be discouraged. If I had to say, interviews are like 60% luck
and 40% skill. Everything ranging from the interviewer’s personality and mood, to the other
candidates shortlisted, is all out of your hands, so don’t be disheartened if you aren’t
selected. Take it in your stride and learn from the experience. It will work out eventually.
For example, there was someone in my batch who gave interviews for almost 7-8 different
companies, before finally getting selected. So don’t worry.
If you do get selected, celebrate! It’s not easy to get selected and requires a lot of effort.
Take a break from everything and enjoy life for some time. Help out your friends who are
still yet to get an offer by taking mock interviews.
If you’ve ever got any questions about my GS interview experience, or about interview prep
in general, feel free to reach out to me at warrenjacinto@gmail.com I will definitely get back
to you as soon as I can.
All the Best!!!
